summary: A 1970 note commenting on RFC 33 and RFC 36, the host-to-host protocol proposals. It updates RFC 36 and offers feedback from its authors.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 44 comments on proposed Host-to-Host protocol rules and recommends changes to reduce complexity. It also records the authors' preferences on padding, character echoing, and a shared character code.

why separate block and close commands
subtitle: Suggestions to simplify connection handling in the proposed Host-to-Host protocol.

tldr.problem: The proposals in RFCs 33 and 36 left questions about reconnection, connection closing, socket tables, padding, echoing, and character conversion.
tldr.mechanism: The authors suggest a local SWITCH call, separate BLOCK and CLOSE commands, and using link numbers in place of foreign socket numbers where possible.
tldr.outcome: The memo records preferences on unresolved issues and updates RFC 36; it is an early discussion document.

today: RFC 44 is listed with status Unknown and updates RFC 36. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 44.

sections.title: Reconnection and Closing
sections.content:
The authors distinguish switching between two sockets at one host from reconnecting to a socket at a foreign host. They consider local switching useful and simple, while foreign reconnection is of uncertain value and needs an elaborate command mechanism.

They recommend leaving foreign reconnection out of the initial protocol and adding a local SWITCH system call. They also propose separate BLOCK and CLOSE commands because the proposed CLOSE command served both to block and abort a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors recommend keeping the first version simpler by supporting local socket switching without foreign reconnection. They also want separate commands for blocking and closing a connection.

sections.title: Links, Sockets, and Ports
sections.content:
Once a connection is established, the authors see no need to retain the foreign socket in a local connection table if a link number corresponds one-to-one with that socket. Most commands could then use the link number, saving a 40-bit foreign socket number in each table entry.

They note that foreign socket numbers would still be needed if connections were multiplexed over links. They also question whether ports add value when they correspond one-to-one with sockets.
sections.plainLanguage: A link number could replace a longer foreign socket number in most commands and table entries. The authors note that different connection arrangements could still require the socket number.

sections.title: Three Open Design Choices
sections.content:
The memo lists three unresolved issues from a UCLA meeting: how to handle padding when a message does not end on a word boundary, whether to echo characters, and where character-code conversion should occur.

The authors prefer shifting the message leader to handle padding, no echoing because it should be managed locally, and a Network Common Code using all 256 characters of an 8-bit code. They suggest ASCII-8 initially, with later expansion according to network needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors state preferences for padding, character echoing, and a shared character code. These are proposals for discussion, not a final protocol specification.

references.text: NWG/RFC 38, proposal concerning multiplexing connections over links.
